newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Albright sees fast track Congress approach soon.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees fast track Congress approach soon.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday the Clinton administration planned to approach Congress "in the very near future" to seek "fast track" authority for trade deals.
But she and other officials said no precise time had yet been decided to seek the authority, a key interest of many Latin American nations.

"We are going to be going to the Hill (Congress) in the very near future to seek that authority and we are looking now at the proper timing of it," Albright told the American Chamber of Commerce in Costa Rica.

President Bill Clinton "had wanted to wait to see if we had a budget deal and that is a process that is ongoing, and we are going to be assessing, obviously, the best time to go to the Hill," Albright said in response to a question.
"But I can just assure you that it is the highest priority and the President has made that quite clear to all of us."
Clinton and Republican leaders agreed last week on a plan to balance the U.S. budget by the year 2002, but the plan still has to be approved by Congress.

At a Latin American summit in Miami in 1994 the three partners in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) -- the United States, Mexico and Canada -- offered Chile the chance to become the fourth member.
The United States, however, has not been able to make good on that invitation because it lacks "fast track," a key authorisation from Congress to negotiate new trade deals.
Treaties signed under that legislation cannot be amended by Congress, which must vote them up or down in a short time.

Clinton's special adviser for Latin America, Thomas "Mack" McLarty, who like Albright is accompanying the president on a Latin American and Caribbean tour, cautioned that a preliminary deal still needed to be struck with Congressional leaders.
"In the past, certain trade legislation has taken four, six years to get passed, in some cases eight," he told the Chamber of Commerce following Albright's remarks.

"I believe we will be successful in fast track. The last thing I think we want to do from a legislative standpoint is to introduce a bill that does not have at least some critical mass, some building of consensus," he said.
"I believe that will be accomplished with (Trade Representative) Ambassador (Charlene) Barshefsky and others in very intensive consultations with the Congress."
Barshefsky and other administration negotiators are holding talks with the Republican majority in Congress to try to find common ground on "fast track" authority.
The Miami summit set a goal of achieving a Free Trade Area of the Americas by 2005, but many Latin American nations are keen to see action sooner than that.

Some U.S. analysts argue that the lack of "fast track" has kept the United States on the sidelines in Latin America and strengthened the hand of Brazil, the leading voice in the Mercosur South American common market agreement.
While NAFTA has not expanded since it started in 1994, Mercosur has struck deals with Chile and Bolivia and is in talks with other South American nations and the European Union.
Clinton is due to visit Brazil and Argentina, Mercosur's main partners, and Venezuela in October.
